title: Quebecor, Telesat exploring partnerships tied to Lightspeed satellite constellation
html:
Ottawa-based satellite company Telesat is developing its low-earth-orbit constellation, Lightspeed.ryan carter/The Globe and Mail

Quebecor Inc. QBR-B-T and satellite operator Telesat Corp. TSAT-T have held exploratory talks about potential partnerships tied to Telesat’s low-earth-orbit satellite constellation, Lightspeed.

The companies, which have had limited discussions until now, engaged in early-stage talks to learn more about what Telesat’s technology can offer and explore potential partnerships, Quebecor told The Globe and Mail in a statement. No investment proposal has been made, the company said.

Telecom and media company Quebecor is currently proposing to buy rival Telus Corp., arguing a combined company would be better able to invest in national networks and compete with Elon Musk’s Starlink, which plans to offer direct-to-device service in the future.

On Monday, while speaking about the proposal, Quebecor president and chief executive officer Pierre Karl Péladeau told The Globe the company could consider making an investment in satellite technology, possibly through a partnership, but stopped short of providing specifics.

“Canada should consider what we will do in the future for our having a proper satellite constellation,” Mr. Péladeau said. “It will make our telecom sovereignty more resilient and more independent, to make sure that at the end of the day, no one’s going to come and say, ‘I switched you off.’”

Quebecor’s Telus proposal has come under scrutiny from competition experts and investment bank analysts, who say it would face significant regulatory hurdles before several levels of government.

It’s not clear whether a potential satellite investment would help resolve anti-competitive concerns. Market concentration of spectrum and mobile subscribers are the main obstacles, according to industry sources.

Telesat declined to comment, saying it does not comment on discussions with prospects, customers or government.

The Ottawa-based satellite company is developing its low-earth-orbit constellation, Lightspeed, and expects global commercial availability in the first quarter of 2028. But the company’s business model is currently designed around business-to-business service, not direct-to-consumer connectivity like Starlink.

Starlink is one of 200 satellite networks that are authorized to operate in Canada, access which is governed by Innovation, Science and Economic Development (ISED) Canada, an ISED spokesperson told The Globe in October.

In Canada, satellite operators can provide direct-to-device service through the use of terrestrial spectrum in the 800 MHz band, which requires a commercial arrangement to be in place between a Canadian mobile network operator and a satellite operator. Already, Starlink has partnered with Rogers Communications Inc. to provide this service.

Satellite providers could also use spectrum bands that are allocated to mobile-satellite service. In May, ISED issued a consultation seeking input on policies related to the use of those bands. It has not yet issued a decision.

While neither of the policies governing this spectrum access include restrictions on foreign ownership, foreign ownership restrictions within the Telecommunications Act could apply, ISED said in a statement.

Moreover, since 2023, ISED has put in place a moratorium which prevents it from considering large transfers of mobile spectrum – the invisible airwaves that carry telecommunications signals – by major licensees. The Minister of Industry approves spectrum transfers under the Radiocommunication Act.

As Ottawa’s policies are intended to prevent the concentration of spectrum licenses among telecom players, any merger between large carriers would face challenges over the consolidation of spectrum.

In addition to this critical roadblock, a Quebecor-Telus merger would face a review before the Competition Tribunal, which would gauge whether the combination would substantially lessen competition, and the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission, which considers broadcast rules.

A merger between Quebecor and Telus would reduce Canada from three independent facilities-based wireless networks to two “unless remedies preserve an equivalent rival,” said Scotiabank analyst Maher Yaghi in a note to investors on Friday.

A win before the Competition Tribunal does not guarantee success, he said. The merger between Rogers and Shaw “showed a deal can win before the Tribunal and still depend on a spectrum decision from the Minister.”

Meanwhile, political will alone is not enough to enable a transaction, he noted.

The Competition Bureau’s work “has been protected over the years and over different political mandates from political interference, and we think the biggest gating factor in this proposed merger is the Bureau’s analysis and conclusions.”
summary: Companies had early-stage talks about the technology but no investment proposal has been made
